brief_angle: When a museum deletes its wall labels, does the information actually disappear or just migrate — and does the deaf visitor end up in a more level room, or in a room whose default channel has quietly become speech (docents, tours, audio guides) with text demoted to atmosphere?
notes: Aphorism budget is blown — I count at least three verdict-sentences competing for the same crescendo: 'Migration is not demotion. It can be the opposite.', 'In a room like that one, the label was the architecture', and 'One is authorship. The other is abdication dressed as generosity.' Keep only the closing line ('...moved the translator's mouth closer') as the piece's single verdict and flatten the other three into plain prose — the Cleveland reversal, for instance, can end on the concrete fact of the resizable text in her pocket, which is stronger than the epigram summarizing it.

Delete the signpost paragraph 'Which is where the thing I keep circling gets uncomfortable.' — the Christine Sun Kim material underneath is the best complication in the piece and it lands harder cold. Same treatment for 'That broke my thesis.' — the Cleveland scene already shows the thesis breaking; announcing it turns a discovery into a technique being demonstrated.

Protect two things in revision: the concession-before-kill in the acoustics paragraph ('There is a position I have argued against for years...') is doing real work — the opposing view gets its strongest form before the flip — and the closing triple juxtaposition (Belvedere study, Philadelphia docent, the friend's Rothko notepad) is the piece's best move, three concrete images clicking with no narration between them. Whatever gets cut, those stay.
